texts.label: text
texts.orig: 2025 downgrade on slower expected demand growth: We leave our current Q4 2024 copper price forecasts unchanged, but see a likelihood of slower 2025 global copper demand and dampened prices as a result of growing trade restrictions. As a result, we have cut our end-2025 price by about 9%.
texts.text: 2025 downgrade on slower expected demand growth: We leave our current Q4 2024 copper price forecasts unchanged, but see a likelihood of slower 2025 global copper demand and dampened prices as a result of growing trade restrictions. As a result, we have cut our end-2025 price by about 9%.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Less trade signals slower demand growth: We have moderately cut our 2025 demand growth expectations from 3.3% to 2.9%. The principal drivers of this revision are our expectations of further contraction in European construction, and in European manufacturing, due to export headwinds. We also expect slower demand growth in China on trade constraints and continued sluggish domestic demand. We remain sceptical that China stimulus measures will offer any meaningful support to copper demand.

The principal drivers of this revision are our expectations of further contraction in European construction, and in European manufacturing, due to export headwinds. We also expect slower demand growth in China on trade constraints and continued sluggish domestic demand. We remain sceptical that China stimulus measures will offer any meaningful support to copper demand.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Copper supply side - robust in 2025: We think strong mine supply growth in 2025, and the commissioning of more smelter capacity, will drive up refined copper supply growth by 3.7% next year, running well ahead of our new demand growth projections. Indeed, we now see an around-500-kt surplus for the copper market next year, roughly a 320 kt increase over our previous 2025 surplus expectations.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: China prices trading at sustained deep discounts to LME: The extent of growth in China's domestic refined copper production has sustained the trend of Chinese physical copper trading at consistently deep discounts to ex-China physical pricing. We see this as a key reason why China's YTD net copper imports have been flat on 2023 volumes, a trend that has effectively pushed the ex-China copper market into oversupply.

texts.orig: LME contango spreads deepest on record: The clearest indication of copper's oversupply has been the trends in the LME forward curve structure, which through October was seeing record contangos, whether looking at cash-3m or longer-dated spreads. Given our expectations of rising surpluses in the global copper market in 2025, we expect deep contango pricing structures to remain a feature of copper over the next year.

texts.orig: Second part of report title China's traditional metals demand drivers increasingly sluggish: Despite numerous policy attempts to stimulate the construction sector, China's property sales, plus commercial and residential property starts and completions, remain very weak, with activity in its third year of contraction. We think there are structural issues at play, namely an aging and shrinking population, the end of rural-urban migration, and the effect of property ceasing to act as a savings or investment vehicle.

texts.orig: Auto production for China's domestic market has continued to slow through 2024. In the year to September, with domestic demand effectively contracting by 3.5%, it is only Chinese vehicle exports, up 28% y/y, that are supporting China's auto sector output growth (+1.9% YTD) and thus auto sector copper demand. This reliance on exports is seen across most Chinese manufacturing sectors.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Second part of report title Trump victory a potential trade, global growth headwind. Global manufacturing has struggled for positive momentum in 2024. The potential implementation of tariffs between 60-100% on US imports from China and Mexico, and 10-20% duties on imports from all other regions, in our view, would act as a headwind to global growth, particularly if other regions impose reciprocal tariffs on US exports. In addition, implementation of tariffs by the US is, in our view, likely to lead to renewed USD strength, presenting a further headwind to USD-denominated metals. We also see a Trump driven partial defunding of the IRA program as a further copper headwind.
texts.text: Second part of report title Trump victory a potential trade, global growth headwind. Global manufacturing has struggled for positive momentum in 2024. The potential implementation of tariffs between 60-100% on US imports from China and Mexico, and 10-20% duties on imports from all other regions, in our view, would act as a headwind to global growth, particularly if other regions impose reciprocal tariffs on US exports. In addition, implementation of tariffs by the US is, in our view, likely to lead to renewed USD strength, presenting a further headwind to USD-denominated metals. We also see a Trump driven partial defunding of the IRA program as a further copper headwind.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: China increasingly reliant on exports for growth: Sluggish domestic demand growth for manufactured products in China has made many sectors more reliant on exports to drive production growth in 2024. Auto manufacturing for China's domestic market has slowed 3.5% YTD, while exports have jumped 28% (Figure 12 above). The same pattern is seen in China's aircon sector (Figure 15) and is a common trend across most manufacturing sectors, heightening tariff risks to China growth.
texts.text: China increasingly reliant on exports for growth: Sluggish domestic demand growth for manufactured products in China has made many sectors more reliant on exports to drive production growth in 2024. Auto manufacturing for China's domestic market has slowed 3.5% YTD, while exports have jumped 28% (Figure 12 above). The same pattern is seen in China's aircon sector (Figure 15) and is a common trend across most manufacturing sectors, heightening tariff risks to China growth.

texts.orig: Second part of report title Accelerating global mine supply: After growth of about 2.0% y/y in 2023, mine supply continued to grow at around 2.4% over the first eight months of 2024. However, we expect copper mine supply to grow by 3.1% this year and about 5% in 2025.
texts.text: Second part of report title Accelerating global mine supply: After growth of about 2.0% y/y in 2023, mine supply continued to grow at around 2.4% over the first eight months of 2024. However, we expect copper mine supply to grow by 3.1% this year and about 5% in 2025.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Our forecast incorporates the closure of Cobre Panama and allows for Anglo American's copper output guidance cuts for 2024. For Chilean output, we see significant upside from the ramp-up of Teck's Quebrada Blanca II and modest upside from improvements at its Ramiro Tomic and Chuqui operations. We also expect continued mine production growth in the DRC and Peru from ongoing project ramp-ups.
texts.text: Our forecast incorporates the closure of Cobre Panama and allows for Anglo American's copper output guidance cuts for 2024. For Chilean output, we see significant upside from the ramp-up of Teck's Quebrada Blanca II and modest upside from improvements at its Ramiro Tomic and Chuqui operations. We also expect continued mine production growth in the DRC and Peru from ongoing project ramp-ups.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Cobre Panama impact limited due to growth elsewhere: We do not expect Cobre Panama to restart for the foreseeable future, but do not see concentrate market deficits or refined-market tightness in 2024/25. This is in part due to significant oversupply in the copper concentrate market for most of 2024 - we estimate well over 300 kt - but also reflects likely mine supply growth in most key copper mining regions and a continuing surge in copper scrap processing in China.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Section A and B services include A. Investment services and activities: (1) Reception and transmission of orders in relation to one or more financial instruments; (2) Execution of orders on behalf of clients; (3) Dealing on own account; (4) Portfolio management; (5) Investment advice; (6) Underwriting of financial instruments and/or placing of financial instruments on a firm commitment basis; (7) Placing of financial instruments without a firm commitment basis; (8) Operation of an MTF; and (9) Operation of an OTF. B. Ancillary services: (1) Safekeeping and administration of financial instruments for the account of clients, including custodianship and related services such as cash/collateral management and excluding maintaining securities accounts at the top tier level; (2) Granting credits or loans to an investor to allow him to carry out a transaction in one or more financial instruments, where the firm granting the credit or loan is involved in the transaction; (3) Advice to undertakings on capital structure, industrial strategy and related matters and advice and services relating to mergers and the purchase of undertakings; (4) Foreign exchange services where these are connected to the provision of investment services; (5) Investment research and financial analysis or other forms of general recommendation relating to transactions in financial instruments; (6) Services related to underwriting; and (7) Investment services and activities as well as ancillary services of the type included under Section A or B of Annex 1 related to the underlying of the derivatives included under points (5), (6), (7) and (10) of Section C (detailing the MiFID II Financial Instruments) where these are connected to the provision of investment or ancillary services.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: BNPP and/or its affiliates understand the importance of protecting confidential information and maintain a "need to know" approach when dealing with any confidential information. Information barriers are a key arrangement we have in place in this regard. Such arrangements, along with embedded policies and procedures, provide that information held in the course of carrying on one part of its business to be withheld from and not to be used in the course of carrying on another part of its business. It is a way of managing conflicts of interest whereby the business of the bank is separated by physical and non-physical information barriers. The Control Room manages this information flow between different areas of the bank where confidential information including inside information and proprietary information is safeguarded. There is also a conflict clearance process before getting involved in a deal or transaction.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In addition, there is a mitigation measure to manage conflicts of interest for each transaction with controls put in place to restrict the information flow, involvement of personnel and handling of client relations between each transaction in such a way that the different interests are appropriately protected. Gifts and Entertainment policy is to monitor physical gifts, benefits and invitation to events that is in line with the firm policy and Anti-Bribery regulations. BNPP maintains several policies with respect to conflicts of interest including our Personal Account Dealing and Outside Business Interests policies which sit alongside our general Conflicts of Interest Policy, along with several policies that the firm has in place to prevent and avoid conflicts of interest.
